stances.claim: Choosing a new president is also choosing a new Supreme Court -- at least 10 of 15 justices reach compulsory retirement age 70 in the next 6 years (potentially 12 if De Castro v JBC or early retirement is invoked), leaving only 3 (Sereno, Leonen, Caguioa) seated, with a possibly lasting jurisprudential impact if young justices are appointed.

De Castro v JBC (March 17, 2010, 9-3) controversially held that Article VII Section 15's midnight-appointments ban does not apply to the SC because of the constitutional 90-day vacancy-filling mandate -- enabling Arroyo to appoint Renato C. Corona as CJ after Puno's May 17, 2010 retirement (within the prohibited period); 2016 offered an alternative via Justice Martin S. Villarama Jr.'s voluntary early retirement Jan 16, 2016 (he was supposed to retire April 14, 2016 within the ban), allowing JBC nomination and Aquino's appointment of Caguioa without ban violation.

Critical to judicial metamorphosis is the JBC vetting nominees -- though headed by the CJ, the JBC can be swayed by the new president who names 5 of 7 members (SOJ ex officio + 4 regular), giving substantial presidential leverage over the nominee pool before the appointment itself.
stances.rhetorical_move: JBC-leverage disclosure (institutional design enables presidential capture)

stances.claim: Beyond the constitutional requirements (proven competence, integrity, probity, independence; natural-born, 40+, 15-year lower-court or law practice), justices must be 'industrious and have a sense of urgency' to handle heavy caseloads -- easily assessed for career jurists via judicial record but requiring a craftable method for noncareer jurists (private practice or academe).

It is now time to weigh legal philosophy of aspiring justices -- the US model where Republican presidents appoint 'originalists, textualists or conservatives' and Democrats appoint 'liberals or progressives' makes new-justice appointments an election issue, as currently exemplified by Obama-Garland-Senate-Republican standoff over the Scalia successor.

At bottom, since the SC's metamorphosis is at stake in the coming polls, presidential candidates should disclose how they would appoint new justices -- making appointment criteria a campaign-disclosure imperative.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban argues that 'the president who will be elected in the May polls can change the composition of the Supreme Court, its legal orientation and, indirectly, its decisions. Thus, choosing a new president is also choosing a new Supreme Court.' At least 10 of the 15 incumbent justices reach the compulsory retirement age of 70 in the next 6 years (2/3 of the full composition), and new appointees could even reach 12. The retirement schedule in chronological order: Perez (Dec 14, 2016), Brion (Dec 29, 2016), Reyes (July 6, 2017), Mendoza (Aug 13, 2017), Velasco (Aug 8, 2018), Leonardo-De Castro (Oct 8, 2018), Del Castillo (July 29, 2019), Jardeleza (Sept 26, 2019), Bersamin (Oct 18, 2019), and Carpio (Oct 26, 2019); two more -- Peralta (March 27, 2022) and Perlas-Bernabe (May 14, 2022) -- retire within the next presidential term ending June 30, 2022. Article VII Section 15 of the Constitution bans presidential appointments two months before the next presidential election through end of term, except temporary executive ones for public service/safety; the SC voted 9-3 in De Castro v JBC (March 17, 2010) that this ban does not apply to the Court because of the 90-day vacancy-filling mandate. This controversial decision enabled then-President Arroyo to name Renato C. Corona CJ after Puno's May 17, 2010 retirement (within the prohibited period). To avoid the controversy, an alternative was found this year when Justice Martin S. Villarama Jr. voluntarily retired early on Jan 16, 2016 (he was scheduled to retire April 14, 2016, within the ban), allowing JBC nomination and Aquino's appointment of Alfredo Benjamin S. Caguioa. If the new president invokes either pathway, he or she could name 12 of 15 justices, leaving only CJ Sereno, Justice Leonen, and Justice Caguioa from the present Court. If the appointees are relatively young (as Arroyo and Aquino did with some appointees), the transformation could leave a lasting jurisprudential impact. Critical too is the JBC, which vets nominees -- though headed by the CJ, it can be swayed by the new president who names 5 of 7 members (SOJ ex officio + 4 regular). The Constitution requires magistrates of 'proven competence, integrity, probity, and independence,' with SC justices natural-born, ≥40 years old, and ≥15 years as lower-court judge or in law practice. CJ adds that justices must be 'industrious and have a sense of urgency' to handle heavy caseload -- assessable from judicial record for career jurists but requiring a craftable method for noncareer ones (private practice, academe). It is also time to weigh legal philosophy -- in the US, Republican presidents appoint 'originalists, textualists or conservatives' and Democrats appoint 'liberals or progressives.' An ongoing controversy is whether Obama should name Antonin Scalia's successor; Obama nominated Merrick B. Garland, but Senate Republicans vowed to 'freeze' the appointment for the next US president to avoid skewing the delicate originalist-liberal balance. 'At bottom, since the metamorphosis of our Supreme Court is at stake in the coming polls, I believe the presidential candidates should disclose how they would appoint new justices.'
